title: Washington's trade-school philosophy
summary: Wilson and Hinton defend Washington's 22 trades as a route out of slavery's lowest labor, noting later critics wanted more liberal arts.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I'm sure you will share my concern and respect for Booker T. knowing from what he had to come to, that he first had to get us in -- not only an education, but in to finding a job. To be waiters and porters and to know how to work -- and this has been misunderstood down through the years.
And it's very unfortunate, you know,

but this was a basic thing -- first you -- I mean, coming out of slavery without any kind of education or any profession, you had to first learn how to do something, and that I think was what this great man was all about.

That's right. Booker T. Washington installed 22 trades at Tuskegee -- there was a machine shop practice, for making metal parts out of machinery; there was auto mechanics; there was printing, on up to newspaper cylinder press; work on up to job printing, on up to linotype operations, architectural drawing, tailoring, just -- cabinet making, regular carpentry, architecture, as I said, architectural drawing -- and just about everything you could think of, to make a living in a more advanced profession than slavery.

It was just picking cotton or working out in the fields, or doing domestic work. Slavery was just the lowest -- but these were actual trades. That's what you would call it -- a trade school to equip the person to do the type of work that eventually leads to joining a union and that sort of work, rather than just the lowest level of manual labor. So that was Booker T's...
Now a lot of people, after he started that thing, began to disagree with Booker T. on that, and thought there should be more emphasis on liberal
But they had to be first this before they could get in academics.
